tz.headline: Tanzania strengthens food security efforts
tz.dek: Officials and stakeholders emphasize resilient food systems beyond just increasing crop production.
paragraphs: Tanzania is enhancing its approach to sustainable food security by focusing on improved seed varieties, agricultural innovation, and stronger extension services. The government is collaborating with the private sector, research institutions, development partners, and farmers to achieve this goal. Stakeholders agree that food security requires more than just increasing crop yields; it necessitates developing resilient food systems capable of facing climate change, pests, and diseases.

Dr. Wilhelm Mafuru, CEO of the National Agricultural Extension Services Agency (NAESA), stated that food security now means ensuring food systems are resilient and serve all communities, not just increasing production. He highlighted that agriculture is vital to Tanzania's economy and livelihoods, with millions depending on it. Dr. Mafuru noted that climate variability, rising input costs, and market disruptions threaten productivity and farmer incomes, underscoring the need for a systemic approach to food security.

Building these resilient food systems involves coordinated efforts such as providing quality seeds, timely extension services, reliable markets, and adequate storage. NAESA, under the Ministry of Agriculture, aims to improve extension services. Bayer Life Science (T) Ltd has promoted drought-tolerant seeds, helping farmers adapt to changing climates. Bayer Communications Business Partner for Crop Science in Africa, Ms. Lisa Bohlmann, noted that Tanzanian smallholder farmers need better access to quality inputs, knowledge, and modern technologies.

tz.headline: Tanzania opens applications for boxing commission leadership
tz.dek: The National Sports Council is accepting applications until November 17th for eight leadership positions within the TPBRC.
paragraphs: The National Sports Council of Tanzania (NSC) has opened applications for leadership roles at the Tanzania Professional Boxing Regulatory Commission (TPBRC). Interested candidates have until November 17th to submit nomination forms for positions including president, vice-president, six zonal representatives, and one women’s representative. Elections are scheduled for November 24th in Dar es Salaam, following candidate interviews on November 20th.

Application fees range from 1m/- for presidential and vice-presidential hopefuls to 200,000/- for zonal and women’s representative candidates. Eligibility criteria for the top two posts require a bachelor’s degree and five years of leadership experience, with former boxers needing three years post-retirement. Zonal representatives need primary education and three years of sports leadership experience in Tanzania.

The zonal positions cover Northern, Southern Highlands, Western, Lake, and Central zones, with specific regions listed for each. All candidates must be Tanzanian citizens aged 18-75 and have no criminal convictions, particularly those involving prohibited substances or illegal sporting methods. Application forms are available at NSC offices and on the council’s website.

ma.headline: Morocco's dams fill as heavy rains hit north
ma.dek: National reservoirs hold 11.21 billion cubic meters of water, reaching 65.82% capacity after storms.
paragraphs: Heavy rain brought up to 40 millimeters of rainfall to parts of northern Morocco this week, prompting authorities to prepare for possible flooding. The General Directorate of Meteorology issued an orange weather warning on Wednesday, expecting another 20 to 35 millimeters of rain in 16 provinces. Hail and strong winds could accompany the storms, which have already affected areas like Ifrane, which recorded 40 millimeters of rain over 24 hours.

Authorities in the Tangier-Tetouan-Al Hoceima region are reinforcing flood precautions, particularly near waterways. Concerns about reservoir operations have also surfaced, though sources dismissed reports of exceptional releases from Oued El Makhazine and Dar Khrofa dams. Oued El Makhazine's daily discharge of approximately 400,000 cubic meters is for electricity generation and irrigation, not an emergency response.

As of November 3, Oued El Makhazine was approximately 65% full and Dar Khrofa around 80.5%. This rainfall arrives as Morocco’s national reservoirs hold 11.21 billion cubic meters of water, reaching 65.82% of their capacity. This is more than double the 31.12% recorded on November 4, 2025, following a prolonged drought.

ma.headline: Morocco job shortfall affects 2.4 million people
ma.dek: Nearly half of young Moroccans aged 15 to 24 face unmet employment needs, according to the High Commission for Planning.
paragraphs: Morocco’s job shortfall impacted 2.4 million people in the third quarter of 2026, with nearly half of young people aged 15 to 24 facing unmet employment needs. The High Commission for Planning (HCP) reported that the national labor underutilization rate reached 19.6% between July and September. Young people faced a 44.5% rate, while women recorded 28.5%.

The 2.4 million affected include the strictly unemployed, those in the potential workforce not currently employed, and underemployed workers, with strict unemployment at 10.5%. The number of people actively seeking work and available rose to 1.22 million, an increase of 103,000 in three months. Paid employment declined by a net 173,000 to 10.47 million people.

Agriculture, forestry and fishing shed a net 145,000 jobs, a 5.6% decrease, while services lost 96,000 jobs. Industry added 69,000 jobs, the only sector to register an increase. Guelmim-Oued Noun region recorded the highest underutilization rate at 38.7%.

ma.headline: Morocco opens Nador West Med container terminal
ma.dek: The new East Terminal features 1,520 metres of quay and aims for 3.5 million TEUs annual capacity by 2030.
paragraphs: Morocco has started operations at the East Terminal of Nador West Med, a port and industrial complex that has drawn 54 billion dirhams (US$5.5 billion) in investment. The East Terminal alone required 5 billion dirhams (US$510 million) and includes 1,520 metres of quay with an 18-metre draft.

The terminal is expected to reach an annual capacity of 3.5 million TEUs by 2030, according to the Ministry of Equipment and Water. A consortium of Marsa Maroc and Terminal Investment Limited will operate the facility for 25 years.

Additional terminals for general cargo, bulk cargo, and roll-on/roll-off units are planned, alongside energy infrastructure including an LNG terminal. This development is part of Morocco’s national port strategy targeting 390 million tons total port capacity by 2030.

ma.headline: Morocco cuts illegal cannabis cultivation by 88%
ma.dek: The Ministry of Interior reported a significant drop in cannabis farming areas from 134,000 hectares in 2003 to 15,496 hectares in 2026.
paragraphs: Morocco has drastically reduced illegal cannabis cultivation, cutting the area by 88.43% since 2003. The land used for this farming fell from approximately 134,000 hectares in 2003 to 15,496 hectares by 2026, according to the Ministry of Interior's performance report.

The ministry attributed this decline to field operations conducted by provincial committees tasked with combating illegal cannabis cultivation. Security operations through August 2026 also resulted in the seizure of over 274 tons of hash, 53 tons of cannabis plants, and significant amounts of other drugs, including cocaine and heroin.

The ministry is intensifying efforts against drug trafficking through enhanced security, training, and expertise exchange, with a focus on emerging drugs and psychotropic pills. Surveillance has increased along borders and coastlines, and awareness campaigns are underway to prevent drug use, especially among youth, with special attention to dealers near schools.

ug.headline: URA operation bullet kills 13-year-old boy in Busia
ug.dek: A UPDF soldier attached to the Uganda Revenue Authority enforcement team fired a shot that killed Dominic Wejuli, aged 13, inside his home.
paragraphs: A 13-year-old boy, Dominic Wejuli, died in Busia district on April 11, 2026, when a stray bullet struck him during a Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) operation. URA enforcement officers were attempting to seize suspected smuggled goods from Kenya stored at a shop in Buhobe trading centre, Bulumbi Sub-county.

Residents reportedly became rowdy and confronted the URA team, attempting to prevent the confiscation of goods. Moses Johnson Mugwe, Bukedi South Police spokesperson, stated that a UPDF soldier fired to disperse the crowd, and a bullet hit Wejuli inside his house. Eyewitness Muhammed Ntalo accused URA of using excessive force and endangering residents.

Harriet Nekesa, the deceased's sister, confirmed Wejuli was a primary four pupil. Resident David Wandera urged URA to review its procedures and prioritize civilian safety, calling for government intervention. Teacher David Ouma also appealed for justice for the bereaved family.

ug.headline: Uganda launches Shs694 billion water project for Greater Kampala
ug.dek: The project will draw water from Lake Victoria to supply over one million people in Wakiso and Mpigi districts.
paragraphs: The Ugandan government has launched a Shs694 billion water and sanitation project to provide safe drinking water to over one million people in Wakiso and Mpigi districts. The Wakiso West Water and Sanitation Project, managed by the National Water and Sewerage Corporation (NWSC), will draw water from Lake Victoria at Bwerenga. It aims to supply areas including Kyengera, Nsangi, Kajjansi, Kasanje, Kiringente, Wakiso Town Council, and Mpigi Town Council.

NWSC Managing Director Dr. Silver Mugisha stated the project addresses the growing demand for water in the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area, which has seen persistent supply challenges due to rapid population growth. The project will increase water production to 62.5 million litres daily and includes 94.2 kilometres of transmission pipelines and 78.5 kilometres of secondary pipelines. Consultants NIRAS A/S and Fichtner GmbH & Co. KG, along with Ugandan firms M&E Associates Ltd and Alliance Consultants Ltd, will handle design and supervision.

The project will also install 941 community water dispensers and yard taps with prepaid meters in informal settlements, benefiting approximately 160,000 residents. This initiative comes as communities like Kyengera have faced intermittent supply, with some households resorting to buying water at Shs1,000 to Shs2,000 per jerrycan.

ug.headline: Uganda agricultural body seeks private partnerships
ug.dek: NARO plans to commercialise research facilities like processing plants and mills to boost revenue.
paragraphs: The National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) in Uganda is exploring public-private partnerships to generate revenue and ensure financial sustainability for agricultural research. The organisation held a top management meeting on November 4, 2026, at Speke Resort Munyonyo to review proposals for commercialising its assets and facilities. These partnerships aim to attract private sector investment, expertise, and technology to maximise the use of NARO’s existing infrastructure.

NARO Director General Dr. Yona Baguma stated that the organisation needs to harness the capacity of its facilities to generate additional resources for research and contribute to national revenue. Identified facilities for commercialisation include a dairy processing plant and livestock feed mill at NaLIRRI, a fish feed mill at NaFIRRI, and a feed sorting facility at Mbarara ZARDI. Hostel facilities at NaFIRRI and MuZARDI are also part of the plan.

Dr. Baguma noted that while government funding remains primary, NARO must diversify its sources as development partner support declines. He highlighted that NARO's annual budget has increased from UGX 61 billion to UGX 223 billion over the past decade, but additional financing is needed. An existing initiative, licensing improved crop varieties, already generates over UGX 1 billion annually.

ug.headline: Uganda Development Bank commits UGX 200 million to COP31
ug.dek: The bank will sponsor the Ugandan Pavilion for the second year, aiming to boost climate action and attract investment.
paragraphs: Uganda Development Bank (UDB) announced its commitment to climate action by sponsoring the Ugandan Pavilion at the upcoming Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, with UGX 200 million. This marks the bank's fourth consecutive participation in the annual UN Climate Conference. The announcement came during a Pre-COP31 National Forum held in Kampala.

Minister of State for Environment Beatrice Anywar stated that the forum was key to consolidating Uganda's priorities in seven negotiation areas, including adaptation, mitigation, and climate finance. She emphasized the need for reliable water sources and predictable weather forecasts for Uganda's agricultural sector. UDB's Director of Economic Research and Knowledge Management, Dr. Francis Mwesigye, highlighted the sponsorship as an investment in showcasing Uganda's climate investment potential.

UDB has established a dedicated Climate Finance Facility (CFF) and Climate Finance Unit, mobilizing over USD 200 million to date. Launched in 2023 with UGX 50 billion in seed capital, the CFF aims to finance bankable climate investments, assess risks, and support projects contributing to emission reduction and economic resilience.

zw.headline: Zimbabwe government cuts exam fee subsidies
zw.dek: From 2028, only BEAM beneficiaries will receive government assistance for Zimsec examination fees.
paragraphs: The Zimbabwean government will phase out universal subsidies for Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (Zimsec) fees, shifting costs to parents. Cabinet approved a revised framework that will maintain support for pupils in rural primary and secondary schools, satellite schools, and those under the Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM) in 2027.

Starting in 2028, only BEAM beneficiaries will receive government assistance for examination fees. This change comes as the government cites mounting fiscal pressures and a need to prioritise vulnerable students. The move will leave other families to shoulder a greater share of national examination costs.

The government's decision to scale back subsidies means families will face increased education expenses. This policy shift impacts the financial planning for parents and guardians responsible for examination fees for their children.

cv.headline: Cape Verde extends voter registration for accessible transport
cv.dek: The National Electoral Commission (CNE) has extended voter registration for its accessible transport program until November 10.
paragraphs: Cape Verde's National Electoral Commission (CNE) has extended voter registration for its accessible transport program until November 10. This program provides free transport for voters with mobility challenges, including the elderly, disabled, and homebound, to reach their polling stations.

The CNE first launched the accessible voting initiative in 2019, aiming to remove barriers for citizens with disabilities and reduced mobility. Previous measures included Braille ballots, sign language in audiovisual materials, and accessibility training for electoral agents. The free transport service was piloted during the May 17, 2026 legislative elections in Praia.

For the upcoming presidential elections on November 15, the CNE plans to expand the free transport service to all municipalities nationwide. This is the second edition of the program, building on the pilot's success in partnership with civil society organizations.

cv.headline: Cape Verde police arrest 20 in drug trafficking sting
cv.dek: Operation Shark nets suspects including police and prison officers in Praia.
paragraphs: Cape Verdean police arrested 20 individuals, including police officers, prison guards, and a public official, on Tuesday, April 3rd, as part of the ongoing Operation Shark. The arrests, conducted by the Central Directorate of Criminal Investigation, target alleged high-risk drug trafficking, money laundering, and criminal association.

The suspects, aged between 20 and 60, are accused of co-perpetrating drug trafficking, conversion, concealment, money laundering, and criminal association. During searches, authorities seized a shotgun, a 6.35mm pistol, ammunition, cannabis, cocaine, cutting agents, and drug preparation paraphernalia. Two vehicles and electronic equipment were also confiscated.

This latest phase follows an initial crackdown on July 16th in Praia, which led to 12 arrests and the seizure of 1.1627 kilograms of cocaine, 2,048,269 Cape Verdean escudos, and 770 euros. The operation aims to dismantle a criminal network believed to have been active for 15 years.

td.headline: Chad security forces receive praise and equipment
td.dek: Police officers in N'Djamena were recognized for arrests and dismantling a criminal network.
paragraphs: Chad's security forces were honored on Monday, November 2, 2026, in N'Djamena for recent successes in combating crime. Director of Public Security, Hachim Haroun Déby, specifically praised three police officers for arresting two wanted criminals in the capital. A local company donated three vehicles, 20 motorcycles, and 50 gas cylinders to support police operations.

Further recognition came after the dismantling of a cross-border criminal network. Agents from Public Security Commissariat No. 16 in Gassi received congratulatory letters from the Minister of Public Security and Immigration for their professionalism. The Director General of the National Police, accompanied by the first deputy prosecutor and a local deputy, visited the Gassi station to acknowledge these efforts.

The Director of Public Security also thanked six officials at Public Security Commissariat No. 8 for their daily commitment. These acknowledgments highlight the attention authorities and the public are giving to security efforts in the capital.

td.headline: Chad trains 34 agents for reproductive health data
td.dek: NGO OASIS-Tchad completed a two-week training for 34 agents in Moundou to collect family planning data.
paragraphs: 34 agents, including 24 female data collectors and 10 team leaders, have been trained to gather reproductive health information in Moundou. The training, organized by NGO OASIS-Tchad under the Family Planning Impact Lab project, concluded on November 4, 2026, after two weeks of capacity building. The agents will now collect data on family planning and reproductive health across Chad.

The closing ceremony in Moundou was led by Dr. Djimadoum Dionadji, the chief medical officer for the Moundou health district. He was joined by Dougssa Rita, the country representative for OASIS-Tchad, and reproductive health focal points from the Logone occidental and Mandoul health delegations. This initiative aims to ensure the collection of reliable data for reproductive health services.
The training began on October 19, 2026, and focused on preparing the selected agents for their fieldwork. The collected data will support family planning efforts in the country.

dj.headline: Djibouti hosts EU security and defence ambassadors
dj.dek: Djibouti's foreign minister and interim interior minister met with EU envoys to discuss security cooperation.
paragraphs: Djibouti hosted ambassadors from the EU's Council of the European Union for Political and Security Committee (COPS) on April 11, 2026. Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdoulkader Houssein Omar and interim Minister of Interior Omar Abdi Said received the delegation led by Ambassador Lene Vensild at the Diplomatic Studies Institute.

The EU COPS delegation represents the bloc's central body for common security and defence policy. Discussions focused on deepening security and military cooperation between Djibouti and the EU, and on regional and international challenges. Both sides described the talks as "in-depth."

Djibouti, located at the entrance to the Bab el-Mandeb strait, is a long-standing partner for Europeans in the Horn of Africa. The visit signifies the importance both Djibouti and the EU place on their partnership and joint initiatives for regional peace and stability.

The handover occurred at the general staff headquarters of the armed forces, attended by Chief of Staff General Zakaria Cheick Ibrahim.

This transfer aligns with the defense cooperation treaty between France and Djibouti and follows joint technical studies by the French forces stationed in Djibouti and the Djiboutian army. A financing agreement signed at the ceremony will fund infrastructure projects to boost the Djiboutian army's operational capabilities.

The defense relationship, strengthened since the treaty's signing on July 24, 2024, saw its first strategic dialogue on June 11, 2026. This dialogue resulted in a two-year partnership plan for 2026-2028.

paragraphs: Somali Parliament Speaker Abdoulkadir Mohamed Nour visited Djibouti's Doraleh Container Terminal and the DIFTZ on March 11, 2026. He was accompanied by Djiboutian National Assembly President Dileita Mohamed Dileita and met with Aboubaker Omar Hadi, president of the Port and Free Zones Authority of Djibouti (APZFD).

At the Doraleh terminal, officials from the Terminal Management Company (SGTD) showcased infrastructure, equipment, and operational capabilities, emphasizing Djibouti's role as a logistics hub in the Horn of Africa. Discussions at the DIFTZ focused on strengthening cooperation between the APZFD and Somali ports.

Djibouti has previously donated two tugboats, the 'Bab el Mandeb' and 'Moussa Bouh', along with container handling equipment to Mogadishu. A Djiboutian technical team was deployed for two years, and port agents received training. In Bossaso, the APZFD conducted bathymetric surveys, improved navigation aids, and provided a tugboat and pushcat, alongside studies on port tariffs and regulations.

sz.headline: Eswatini farmers urged to sell livestock as drought kills over 50 cattle
sz.dek: Shiselweni Region faces severe water and pasture shortages, impacting livestock health and productivity.
paragraphs: Farmers in Eswatini's Shiselweni Region are being urged to sell their livestock as over 50 cattle have died due to drought conditions. The figure was revealed at an emergency stakeholder meeting in Nhlangano yesterday. Severe shortages of grazing pasture and drinking water have led to poor cattle body conditions, increased drought-related abortions, and reduced productivity.

Shiselweni Regional Veterinary Officer Dr. Allen Simbai Maruve stated that Hluti reported 10 to 20 cattle deaths in the worst-affected communities, with Lavumisa experiencing more than 20 deaths. Dip tanks in Hluti, such as Tsekwane and Qomintaba, face critical stress, while Lavumisa faces acute livestock water shortages impacting multiple dip tanks. Common challenges include pasture depletion, drying water sources, and increased disease susceptibility.

Dr. Maruve called for immediate emergency assistance over the next three months, including feed support like hay bales and mineral licks, and water support such as tankers and rehabilitation of water points. Medium-term priorities include water infrastructure development, borehole drilling, and solar-powered pumping systems.

The ECA stated that Jele's new qualification will help elevate the standard of cricket across Eswatini. The association praised the ESRC for its commitment to sports development in the country. Jele previously represented Eswatini on the pitch for six years before moving into coaching roles.

sz.headline: Eswatini court hears explosive found in South Africa
sz.dek: Assistant Superintendent Bhekani Shiba testified that a device was collected from Bonginkhosi IB Dlamini’s home in South Africa.
paragraphs: An explosive device allegedly found with businessman Zweli Dlamini was collected from Bonginkhosi IB Dlamini’s home in South Africa, Assistant Superintendent Bhekani Shiba testified yesterday. Shiba stated that Zweli, a member of PUDEMO, communicated with activist Samora Ginindza before collecting the device. Zweli faces charges under the Suppression of Terrorism Act and Explosives Act before Judge Sabelo Masuku.

Shiba, Head of the Counter-Terrorism and Organised Crime Unit, told the court that police investigations established Zweli travelled to South Africa on December 19, 2025, and returned the next day. Zweli allegedly explained to police that he was instructed to transport the explosive device from South Africa into Eswatini. Two names, Samora Ginindza and Bonginkhosi IB Dlamini, emerged during the accused’s interview as comrades with knowledge of the items.

The investigation into Zweli Dlamini began on December 22, 2025, after Superintendent Derrick Makhanya informed Shiba of the arrest. Intelligence suggested the explosives were intended to disrupt the Incwala Ceremony. Shiba has nearly 20 years of experience in terrorism investigations and has handled over 500 such cases.

sz.headline: Eswatini football squad announcement delayed
sz.dek: The Eswatini Football Association has failed to name the Sihlangu Semnikati team for a friendly against Malta.
paragraphs: The Eswatini Football Association (EFA) has not yet announced the Sihlangu Semnikati squad for an upcoming international friendly against Malta, despite promising to do so by Tuesday. The team was scheduled to depart for the match against the European nation, set for November 12, 2026, in Ta’ Qali. This fixture marks the first time Eswatini will play a friendly against a European country.

EFA Marketing and Communications Manager Muzi ‘Rhoo’ Radebe stated he was awaiting the executive committee's decision on the squad. He admitted on Tuesday that he had received no update and remained unaware of any new timeline for the announcement. The EFA had previously confirmed concluding engagements with the Malta Football Association (MFA) for the match.

sz.headline: MP fears drought will leave patients hungry
sz.dek: Shiselweni I MP Shawnette Henwood questioned hospital preparedness for a potential El Niño drought and its impact on patient nutrition.
paragraphs: Shiselweni I MP Shawnette Henwood questioned whether hospitals can support patients facing food shortages during a possible drought. Henwood raised the concern during debate on the Ministry of Health’s second-quarter performance report, asking if the ministry had prepared for a possible El Niño-related drought and its effects on patients who depend on medication. She recalled that the ministry previously provided food to some patients and asked why the programme had ended, wanting to know what assistance would be available if drought conditions made it difficult for patients to obtain food.

Legislators also called for dialysis services at more hospitals to reduce patients’ journeys to Mbabane Government Hospital, citing non-operational dialysis machines at some public facilities. Sithobelweni MP Vincent Sihlongonyane questioned why antivenom appeared to be available at certain hospitals but not others, noting that high temperatures in his constituency increased concerns about snakebites. Nkomiyahlaba MP Mantunta Dlamini and LaMgabhi MP Sicelo Jele also called for wider availability of antivenom as temperatures rose.

Health Minister Mduduzi Matsebula responded to questions about dialysis, stating that machines would begin operating later in the month. Henwood also raised concerns about access to cancer treatment, pointing to a backlog of cases involving patients awaiting support from the Phalala Fund and calling for intervention. She also asked when bagcugcuteli would receive their proposed allowance increase.

ga.headline: Gabon signs Accra Convention for digitized cargo documents
ga.dek: The treaty aims to simplify trade by allowing electronic transfer of ownership rights and reducing paperwork for multimodal transport.
paragraphs: Gabon signed the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents, known as the Accra Convention, in Accra, Ghana, on Monday, October 26, 2026. The Ministry of Transport announced that the treaty establishes common rules for issuing and using cargo documents in paper or electronic formats across all transport modes.

This convention allows ownership rights in goods to be transferred by their representing document, facilitating the sale of cargo in transit and trade finance. It also permits a single negotiable document for multimodal transport, reducing administrative burdens and the risk of lost or forged paperwork for Gabonese businesses.

The agreement supports ongoing reforms, including a proposal to digitize administrative documents and improve road freight tracking discussed in January 2026. Gabon must ratify the convention and incorporate its provisions into national law, with further steps needed to integrate systems and ensure business adoption of new tools.

ga.headline: Gabon firms sign iron ore rail deal
ga.dek: REMINAC and SETRAG will negotiate transport of Baniaka iron ore to Owendo port.
paragraphs: Gabon's Baniaka iron ore project has moved forward with a memorandum of understanding signed on October 28, 2026, in Libreville. REMINAC, which is developing the project, and SETRAG, the railway operator, agreed to negotiate the transport of future iron ore production by train to the port of Owendo. This agreement aims to structure the logistics for the project, which is expected to boost Gabon's mining potential.

The deal will lead to discussions on ore flow scheduling, transport capacity on the Transgabonais railway, potential infrastructure work, and pricing and commercial terms. SETRAG's director general, Christian Magni, stated the collaboration aligns with the Transgabonais' role in supporting the country's economic sectors.

Genmin, the group overseeing the Baniaka project, has invested approximately $120 million USD in its development. Thierry Makando, Genmin's country director, stated the signing is an important step towards realizing the Baniaka project, emphasizing the need for a reliable and cost-effective logistics solution to support production startup.

ga.headline: Gabon signs carbon credit deal for 6 million tonnes
ga.dek: Gabon becomes the first African nation to sell certified forest preservation credits eligible for international aviation emissions compensation.
paragraphs: Gabon has signed its first agreements to sell jurisdictional carbon credits, committing to approximately 6 million tonnes of CO2 with Germany's state-owned energy company SEFE. The deals, announced on November 3, 2026, by the Presidency's spokesperson Théophane Nzame-Nze Biyoghe, aim to generate new revenue streams from forest preservation. First deliveries are expected by the first quarter of 2027.

These credits are certified under the ART-TREES standard and are eligible for CORSIA, the international aviation emissions compensation mechanism. The transactions are described as 'jurisdictional', meaning they are accounted for at a national or administrative territory level. Gabon's government stated that the country is not selling its land or forests, but rather carbon units, with ownership and management remaining with the state.

The financial details of the agreements, including the price per tonne and the total expected revenue, were not disclosed in the announcement. The net sums returning to the state will depend on the negotiated financial terms and distribution arrangements. The revenues will be held in a dedicated account until a national regulatory framework is established.

gm.headline: Gambia launches two projects to restore ecosystems
gm.dek: The Great Green Wall RECOSERV Gambia Project and FARM-Plus Project aim to combat land degradation and deforestation.
paragraphs: The Gambia launched two five-year projects on Tuesday to restore degraded ecosystems and promote sustainable agriculture. The Great Green Wall (GGW) RECOSERV Gambia Project and the FARM-Plus Project were initiated to combat climate change, deforestation, and land degradation. These initiatives are funded by the Global Environment Facility (GEF) with support from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), and will be executed by the National Environment Agency (NEA).

The RECOSERV Gambia project aims to restore 43,000 hectares of forest and wetland ecosystems, improve management across 38,000 hectares of protected areas, and introduce sustainable practices on 36,000 hectares of rural landscapes. These interventions are expected to benefit approximately 795,000 people, primarily women. FAO Country Representative Moshibudi Rampedi stated that the projects will help farmers adopt alternatives that reduce harmful chemicals, conserve water, and minimize waste.

Minister of Agriculture Demba Sabally described the projects as a commitment to combating desertification and securing agricultural land productivity. The FARM-Plus project will focus on strengthening policies, improving access to finance and insurance, building technical capacity, and promoting sustainable value chains for climate-smart agriculture. Minister of Environment Rohey John Manjang emphasized that success will be measured by the survival of restored forests and tangible improvements in livelihoods.

gm.headline: Gambia election nominations face early hurdles
gm.dek: One party withdrew while two aspirants encountered issues with documentation and fees on the first day of nominations.
paragraphs: The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) began receiving presidential nominations for the December 5, 2026 election on Tuesday, November 3, in Kanifing. The All-Inclusive Party withdrew its aspirant from the scheduled nomination, and two other candidates faced immediate challenges. The nomination process, which continues until November 14, requires aspirants to deposit D1 million into an IEC-designated account and provide original citizenship documents.

Independent candidate Salieu Jallow could not complete his nomination after failing to meet the D1 million deposit requirement, misunderstanding the payment process. Modou Lamin Sima, presidential aspirant for the Alliance of Progressive Citizens, submitted photocopies of his citizenship documents instead of originals, risking rejection unless he provides the required originals before the window closes. IEC Chairman Joseph Colley stated that original documents are mandatory under the Elections Act 2025.

The tightened compliance regime under the Elections Act 2025, including the D1 million deposit, has sparked public debate. Proponents argue it ensures seriousness and covers electoral costs, while critics contend it creates barriers for independents and smaller parties. The election will be the first under this revised electoral framework, which raises nomination thresholds.

gm.headline: UNITE accuses gov't of misrepresenting report
gm.dek: The party claims the government's White Paper distorts findings to disqualify presidential candidate Mayor Talib Ahmed Bensouda.
paragraphs: The UNITE coalition has accused the Gambian government of deliberately misrepresenting a Commission of Inquiry report to influence the upcoming elections and disqualify its presidential candidate, Mayor Talib Ahmed Bensouda. UNITE Secretary for Legal and Constitutional Affairs, Abdul Aziz Bensouda, stated at a press conference that the government's White Paper distorts the commission's findings.

Bensouda argued that the White Paper does not reflect the actual report, which he said contains no disqualifying findings against the mayor. He noted that an adverse finding served in May stated only that the mayor had "exercised political and executive influence in a manner capable of causing or sustaining irregular commitments, unauthorised expenditure, irregular project direction, and extra-statutory financial exposure," which he contended does not amount to corruption or misconduct.

UNITE also alleged that the report was altered after its May submission to the President, with metadata showing changes, and suggested parts may have been generated by artificial intelligence. The party claims the government is politicising the report's release ahead of nominations to use state resources to influence the 2026 elections and warned of rising political tensions.

gm.headline: NAWEC warns of fines for illegal electricity connections
gm.dek: The national water and electricity company identified 200 bypass connections and 400 faulty meters, with penalties set at D50,000 for domestic and D200,000 for business users.
paragraphs: The National Water and Electricity Company (NAWEC) is warning individuals involved in electricity theft through illegal connections and meter bypasses that they will face financial penalties and possible prosecution. NAWEC's Managing Director, Gallo Saidy, announced at a town hall meeting in MansaKunda that the company has identified approximately 200 electricity bypass connections and about 400 cases of faulty meters.

A task force has been established to conduct nationwide operations to identify these irregularities. Domestic users caught bypassing electricity will be charged around D50,000, while businesses face charges of approximately D200,000. Those found guilty will also face court action as NAWEC works to combat theft and protect its infrastructure, which has also suffered damage during recent demonstrations.

Mr. Saidy urged Gambians to protect NAWEC facilities, stating that vandalism and illegal connections hinder reliable service delivery. He also cautioned consumers against using substandard electrical materials, as poor wiring can cause safety risks and electricity problems. The company relies on consumer cooperation to report irregularities and improve services across the country.

Barry called for judicial proceedings to establish criminal responsibility.

paragraphs: Mamady Doumbouya now leads both the Guinean Football Federation (FÉGUIFOOT) and the Telecommunications Regulation Authority (ARPT). He was elected FÉGUIFOOT president on October 27 and has directed ARPT since May 8, 2023.

This dual role faces scrutiny under Guinean law. Article 18 of the telecommunications law states the ARPT director general cannot hold elected office. FÉGUIFOOT statutes do not explicitly forbid this position.
The legal compatibility of Doumbouya's positions remains unclear. The law prohibits the ARPT director from holding any elected national or local mandate.

gn.headline: CRIEF summons officials in 3.135 tonnes gold case
gn.dek: Four personalities, including the current central bank governor, will testify on November 23 regarding alleged gold embezzlement.
paragraphs: The Court for the Repression of Economic Offenses (CRIEF) has summoned four individuals to appear as witnesses in the trial of former central bank governor Lounceny Nabé. Current central bank governor Dr. Karamo Kaba, former vice-governor Abdoulaye Yéro Baldé, legal director Daouda Diané, and Mamady Condé, Affinor's representative in Guinea, are expected in court on November 23.

Lounceny Nabé faces charges of embezzling public funds amounting to 3.135 tonnes of gold, illicit enrichment, and corruption. Nabé denies the accusations, stating the gold, valued at approximately $180 million, remains with Affinor, the company contracted for its refining since 2015. The court ordered the witnesses' appearance at the request of the special prosecutor and the defense to clarify the contract's conclusion and execution.
The case was adjourned to November 23, 2026, for the witnesses' testimony. The trial concerns the alleged diversion of public funds and corruption linked to a gold refining contract.

gw.headline: Guinea-Bissau falls behind on UEMOA reforms
gw.dek: The Secretary of State for the Treasury admitted a slight setback in implementing community policies and projects.
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau has seen a slight decline in its implementation of reforms, policies, and projects for the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA), according to Treasury Secretary Justino Vieira. He stated on November 4, 2026, that the results were less satisfactory than those recorded in 2024.

Vieira emphasized the need for better coordination between national authorities and technical departments to transpose UEMOA directives. The 12th annual evaluation, taking place in Bissau from November 4-6, aims to assess reform execution and find ways to strengthen national ownership of the sub-regional organization's initiatives.

The government aims to improve the implementation of UEMOA's additional acts and regulations, speed up directive transposition, and enhance the execution quality of funded programs. UEMOA Resident Representative Aly Coulibaly noted that the evaluation's modalities were set in Bamako, Mali, in June.

gw.headline: US-funded vaccine trial cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
gw.dek: Accusations of unethical and neocolonial practices led to the cancellation of a hepatitis B vaccine trial on newborns.
paragraphs: A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine for newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled. Police seized a batch of vaccines from the Bandim Health Project research centre, which has operated in the country since 1978. The trial was funded by the US under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.

The trial faced international criticism for planning to withhold a World Health Organization-recommended vaccine from half of the participating newborns. Some public health experts questioned whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being subjected to risks not accepted in wealthier nations. The US department of health and human services has been asked for comment.
Guinea-Bissau, like many neighbouring countries, typically waits until babies are six weeks old for hepatitis B vaccination, while the WHO recommends vaccination at birth.

gw.headline: Guinea-Bissau debt hits 76.9% of GDP
gw.dek: Prime Minister Té acknowledges fiscal pressure despite projected GDP growth of 5.2% for 2026.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Ilídio Vieira Té stated on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, in Bissau that Guinea-Bissau's public debt has reached 76.9% of its GDP. He also noted that the current fiscal pressure of 9.1% is insufficient to meet the state's financing needs.

Speaking at a press conference with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Té called for greater financial discipline, modernization of tax and customs administration, and increased transparency in public management. He highlighted that GDP is expected to grow by 5.2% in 2026 and 5.8% in 2027, with the budget deficit projected to fall from 7% in 2025 to 4.2% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027.

The IMF mission is in the country to finalize the review of an economic and financial program started in 2023 and to negotiate a new agreement. IMF mission chief Niko Hobdari reported that inflation has dropped to 0.7% and recommended strengthening tax collection and the financial sector.

gw.headline: Lawyers accuse Supreme Court judges of crimes
gw.dek: A group of lawyers filed a criminal complaint against the former president and two counselors of the Supreme Court of Justice.
paragraphs: A collective of lawyers filed a criminal complaint on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with the Public Prosecutor's Office against members of the leadership of the Supreme Court of Justice (STJ). The complaint targets former STJ president Lima André and counselors Arafam Mané and João Mendes Pereira, who are accused of several crimes.

Lawyer Nansambe stated that the complaint stems from accusations by citizens Marcelino Intupe and Ussumane Sanhá, and called for an investigation into the facts. Intupe listed alleged crimes including obstruction of justice, usurpation of public functions, dereliction of duty, denial of justice, embezzlement, malicious denunciation, qualified damages, and forgery. Mané was also accused of suspending judges and cases without proper justification.
The lawyers are seeking accountability for the accused if the charges are proven. Marcelino Intupe urged the Public Prosecutor's Office to investigate the case and determine any responsibilities.

gw.headline: Guinea-Bissau scientists push for sardinella management plan
gw.dek: Researchers advocate for full implementation of a plan to protect vital fish stocks, approved over a year ago.
paragraphs: Researchers in Guinea-Bissau are urging the full implementation of a Sardinella Fisheries Management Plan, approved more than a year ago, to preserve the country's fish resources. The call came during a two-day seminar in Bissau on November 4, 2026, focused on lessons learned from a sustainable sardinella management project.

The seminar, funded by the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) through the EAF-Nansen Programme and involving the National Network of Community Radios (RENARC) and the National Institute of Fisheries and Oceanographic Research (INIPO), aims to identify project challenges and strengthen partner commitment. INIPO researcher Cadidjatu Djaló stated the institute remains available to collaborate on protecting this fundamental resource.

RENARC president Demba Sanhá explained his organization's role in communicating and raising awareness among local communities over the past 18 months. The meeting will review activities and formulate recommendations for INIPO and FAO.

lr.headline: Liberian importers petition legislature over shipping delays
lr.dek: Business owners face seven-month cargo delays and rising port fees, petitioning for intervention.
paragraphs: Liberian business owners and importers gathered Tuesday at the Capitol Building in Monrovia to petition the Legislature and the National Port Authority over severe shipping delays and increased port fees. The groups, including China Business Women United with One Voice and the Consortium of Liberia Importers, are demanding urgent intervention as cargo shipments from Asia now take six to seven months to reach the Freeport of Monrovia.

Advocate Sriya Musu Momolu stated that these prolonged shipping timelines and unfair fees are pushing local enterprises to the brink of collapse. Businesses relying on bank loans fear losing personal homes and properties due to accumulating interest rates caused by the delays. The petition highlights that Delivery Orders arbitrarily expire before cargo can be retrieved, forcing owners to pay costly renewal fees and demurrage charges for delays beyond their control.

The House of Representatives has summoned key maritime and shipping stakeholders for a hearing on Friday, November 6, following the protest. Importers are also complaining about administrative surcharges and double taxation, as loan interest accumulates while they must still meet tax obligations to the Liberia Revenue Authority and pay salaries.

lr.headline: Liberia tells IMO seafarers must not be war targets
lr.dek: Liberia's Maritime Commissioner Neto Zarzar Lighe, Sr. voiced concern over attacks in key shipping lanes.
paragraphs: Liberia has urged the International Maritime Organization (IMO) that seafarers should not be targeted in ongoing conflicts affecting global shipping lanes. Maritime Commissioner and CEO Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe, Sr. stated this on Tuesday, November 3, at the IMO Council's 138th session, highlighting grave concerns over persistent attacks in the Black Sea, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and other critical waterways. Thousands of seafarers and their vessels are currently trapped by military operations in these waters.

Commissioner Lighe stressed that seafarers are innocent civilians whose work is essential for international trade and the global economy, and they must not become casualties of geopolitical hostilities. He noted that these "unwarranted attacks" endanger crews, damage vessels, disrupt trade, and have tragically claimed lives. Liberia extended condolences to the families of seafarers killed in these incidents.

Liberia's plea carries significant weight as it is the world's largest ship registry, representing about 17 percent of the global fleet. Ships flying the Liberian flag have been directly affected by attacks, including the Liberian-flagged Express Rome struck on March 11 and the Minoan Pioneer hit by a projectile on August 3. The Liberian Maritime Authority has ordered its flagged ships to the highest security level following these events.

lr.headline: Liberia ex-NSA official gets 50 years for statutory rape
lr.dek: Peter Bon Jallah, 63, was sentenced Tuesday, November 3, for statutory rape of a 16-year-old boy.
paragraphs: Former National Security Agency official Peter Bon Jallah, 63, was sentenced to 50 years in prison on Tuesday, November 3, for the statutory rape of a 16-year-old boy. Criminal Court “E” Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. handed down the sentence at the Monrovia Central Prison. Jallah was convicted of statutory rape following weeks of legal proceedings.

The court acquitted Jallah of gang rape, stating insufficient evidence, but his kidnapping conviction was quashed due to jurisdictional error and will be pursued in a new trial. Prosecutors presented 12 witnesses, including DNA evidence, though the forensic examiner noted it could not establish when the biological material was deposited. Jallah was arrested in January 2026.

Jallah’s defense lawyer announced plans to appeal the conviction and sentence to the Supreme Court of Liberia. The case has drawn public attention due to Jallah's former position and the involvement of a minor. The judge denied Jallah’s motion for a new trial.

lr.headline: Liberian businesswomen protest port delays
lr.dek: Hundreds of women marched to the Capitol Building demanding government action on shipping and port charges.
paragraphs: Liberian businesswomen protested at the Capitol Building on Tuesday, November 3, against prolonged shipping delays and excessive port charges. They warned that their businesses are on the verge of collapse due to these issues, which also include alleged violations of Liberia’s Liberianization Policy. The women, many dressed in white, carried placards highlighting their plight and demanding urgent government intervention.

Protesters accused shipping companies like Maersk Line of significant cargo delivery delays, leading to expired delivery orders and mounting bank loan obligations. Madam Matherline Nimely stated that shipments from Asia now take six to seven months to arrive in Monrovia, preventing inventory replenishment. She explained that entrepreneurs face high-interest payments on loans secured with their properties while their goods remain stranded.

Legislators, including Representative Prince Toles and Senator Abraham Darius Dillon, received the petition and pledged to examine the concerns. They assured the businesswomen that legislative efforts to address shipping and port challenges were already underway, with invitations extended to relevant stakeholders. The lawmakers stated they would act on the presented document.

lr.headline: Liberia explores bamboo for eco-prosperity
lr.dek: Liberian experts suggest adapting China's bamboo model to boost local economies and manage natural resources.
paragraphs: Liberian media representatives visited Anji County, China, to observe how bamboo processing, conservation, and rural tourism have transformed the local economy. This visit aims to inform Liberia's approach to managing its forests, wetlands, and agricultural landscapes for employment and community benefit.

Researchers Forkpah Pewee and Dr. Anthony Saah Tengbh believe elements of Anji's model can work in Liberia if adapted to local conditions and supported by practical investments. China's policy, launched after President Xi Xiapin's 2020 UN speech, promotes bamboo as a biodegradable substitute for plastic to combat climate change and pollution.

Liberia, with its extensive natural resources, could potentially turn conservation into a foundation for prosperity. However, successful implementation will depend on financing, infrastructure, technical capacity, environmental enforcement, and community ownership, according to the report.

ly.headline: Libyan publishers face rising book costs
ly.dek: Imported paper and fluctuating exchange rates drive up production expenses for local bookmakers.
paragraphs: Libyan publishers are grappling with increased book production costs due to reliance on imported paper and fluctuating foreign currency exchange rates. These economic pressures are affecting both the local publishing industry and the affordability of books for Libyan readers.

Ali Jaber, manager of Al-Jaber Publishing, stated that printing costs are similar across Libya, Egypt, and Tunisia because all presses use imported paper. He explained that publishers often price books based on the US dollar's parallel market rate, as they cannot open official letters of credit for imports. Producing a book that cost $5 (7.5 dinars) in 2010 now costs nearly 50 dinars.

While Libyan titles are generally priced lower than imported Arab books, ranging from 30 to 50 dinars, rising costs have reduced publisher revenues. Shipping books from Cairo to Benghazi can be cheaper than between some Libyan cities, costing about 100 dinars per parcel, though cross-border shipments can take up to 45 days.

ly.headline: Libya allows imports using parallel market currency
ly.dek: The Ministry of Economy and Trade issued a decree permitting temporary use of foreign currency from the parallel market for goods importation until March 31, 2027.
paragraphs: Libya's Ministry of Economy and Trade announced on April 11, 2026, that goods can be imported using foreign currency from the parallel market. Minister Suhail Abu Shiha issued Decree No. (555) of 2026, allowing this on a temporary basis until March 31, 2027, subject to legal regulations.

The ministry stated this U-turn aims to regulate import operations and oversee trade financing, excluding certain essential goods and medicines that require prior approval. This decision follows previous attempts to restrict imports through bank payments, which were previously reversed.

The current system of documentary letters of credit is seen as unequal, dominated by a few large businesses that obtain most hard currency. These businesses are perceived to be in collusion with bank officials, leaving small and medium-sized enterprises unable to secure funding through official channels and forcing them to use the parallel market.

mg.headline: Madagascar court allows constitutional referendum before presidential vote
mg.dek: The High Constitutional Court ruled that a referendum to adopt a new constitution can proceed before the presidential election.
paragraphs: Madagascar's High Constitutional Court (HCC) ruled on November 4, 2026, that a referendum to adopt a new constitution can be held before the presidential election. The court, responding to a request from the President of the Refoundation, determined that a popular consultation for a new constitution does not violate current constitutional provisions.

The HCC clarified that while a simple revision of the existing text is different from adopting a new constitution to establish a new institutional order, the latter is legally possible. This process would begin with the President of the Refoundation, followed by a Council of Ministers deliberation. The proposed constitution would then require approval from three-quarters of the National Assembly members before being submitted to a popular vote.

The project law for 2027 allocates over 199 billion ariary to the CENI for electoral preparations, including the constitutional referendum and presidential election. The HCC also stated that a referendum offering multiple options to voters is feasible, provided that legal and regulatory frameworks are amended beforehand. The official electoral calendar is yet to be established.

mg.headline: Russia and US intensify influence efforts in Madagascar
mg.dek: Both nations are increasing diplomatic and security engagements across the island nation.
paragraphs: Madagascar is experiencing heightened diplomatic activity from both Russia and the United States, with both powers increasing contacts on military, security, and economic fronts. Recent visits by representatives from both nations to the northern part of the island highlight this growing competition for influence in the Indian Ocean region.

Military cooperation is a key area of focus between Madagascar and Russia, with plans to continue training Malagasy soldiers by Russian instructors and exchange defense equipment. Discussions also cover agriculture, health, higher education, and mining governance. Meanwhile, U.S. officials from AFRICOM, led by General John Brennan, met with Malagasy leaders on November 3-4 to discuss maritime surveillance, combating illicit trafficking, piracy, and military training, alongside the importance of critical minerals for economic security.

Russian interim chargé d'affaires Alexeï Buriak visited Nosy Be to discuss tourism, agriculture, and trade in vanilla and ylang-ylang essential oils, renewing an agreement on maintaining Russian monuments. The U.S. delegation's visit focused on maritime security and critical minerals, indicating a strategic interest in Madagascar's resources and location.

mg.headline: Madagascar parliament to review 2027 budget
mg.dek: The finance bill proposes 5.1% economic growth and targets energy, roads, agriculture, education, and health.
paragraphs: Madagascar's National Assembly will examine the 2027 finance bill, which outlines the government's economic recovery ambitions. The Ministry of Economy and Finance submitted the draft law on time, allowing deputies to review the economic and budgetary choices. This submission adheres to institutional procedures and prioritizes parliamentary debate.

The 2027 budget, prepared under the guidance of Minister Dr. Ramiarison Herinjatovo Aimé, aims for 5.1% economic growth, up from an estimated 4.1% in 2026. Key priorities include revitalizing the energy sector, particularly the Jirama company, improving road infrastructure, and supporting agriculture, education, and health. The budget also allocates funds for a constitutional referendum and presidential elections planned for 2027.

The government plans to strengthen fiscal discipline by increasing tax and customs revenue collection and combating fraud. Public spending will focus on investments expected to yield concrete economic and social returns. Regional budget conferences have helped identify territorial priorities for the decentralization agenda.

mg.headline: Madagascar central bank holds key rate at 12.50%
mg.dek: The Bank of Madagascar will maintain its benchmark interest rate at 12.50% for three months to combat rising inflation.
paragraphs: The Central Bank of Madagascar (BFM) decided to keep its benchmark interest rate at 12.50% following a monetary committee meeting on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. This decision, effective November 4 for three months, aims to continue fighting inflation which is impacting household purchasing power and economic activities.

The BFM's monetary policy report on November 3 stated that maintaining this rate will help keep monetary conditions restrictive enough to gradually bring inflation back to its 5% medium-term target. Annual inflation rose to 8.6% in September from 6.8% in March, driven by food and energy prices.

The central bank forecasts inflation could reach 9.3% in December 2026 before slowing in the second quarter of 2027. This sustained high rate may increase borrowing costs for Malagasy businesses, particularly SMEs needing finance for investments, and could also make credit less accessible for households.

mw.headline: Malawi allows private power producers to feed grid
mw.dek: New net-metering rules let individuals and companies sell surplus renewable energy to the national grid.
paragraphs: Malawi's Energy Minister Jean Mathanga launched new net-metering rules in Lilongwe on Wednesday, allowing private entities to feed surplus electricity from renewable sources into the ESCOM national grid. The country currently generates 564 megawatts, which falls short of rising demand. Mathanga stated that new approaches are needed to increase electricity generation and improve access to reliable power.

The pilot phase of the net-metering initiative identified 34 customers eligible to connect to the national grid, with nine already connected. Minister Mathanga also introduced policies to encourage electric vehicle adoption, which could help ease fuel shortages and lessen dependence on imported fuel. She urged Malawians to protect electricity infrastructure.

Managing Director for Sky Energy Schizzo Thomson said public awareness of electric vehicles could help cut transport costs. The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) has threatened demonstrations over the fuel supply crisis, demanding the resignation of Minister Mathanga, who identified a shortage of foreign exchange as the root cause.

mw.headline: Malawi state firms lose K640 billion
mw.dek: World Bank report highlights weak cash flows and declining dividends from government-owned enterprises.
paragraphs: Malawi's state-owned enterprises (SOEs) are financially weak and rely heavily on government support, according to the World Bank's 23rd Malawi Economic Monitor. These parastatals face weak cash flows, struggle to service debts, and contribute declining dividends to the government. The World Bank's analysis, presented in Lilongwe last week, found that SOEs routinely provide goods and services below cost-recovery levels, leading to debt accumulation and reduced service quality.

The hidden costs from these quasi-fiscal activities amount to K640 billion, equivalent to two percent of Malawi's gross domestic product (GDP). Between 2022 and 2025, commercial SOEs received K292.17 billion in government grants alone. Minister of Finance Joseph Mwanamvekha acknowledged the financial weakness and inefficiency but noted that some SOEs perform essential social functions.

Despite a significant expansion in the SOE sector, with total assets rising from 14 percent of GDP in 2019 to 26 percent in 2024, performance has not improved. The World Bank identified technical losses, overstaffing, weak revenue collection, and governance flaws as the true drivers of this decay. Regulatory parastatals, funded by mandatory fees, remain the only consistent performers.

mw.headline: Malawi mourns poet Jack Mapanje
mw.dek: The writer, known for exploring freedom and power, died in the United Kingdom.
paragraphs: Distinguished Malawian poet, linguist, and academic Jack Mapanje has died in the United Kingdom. Mapanje, born on March 25, 1944, built an international reputation for his metaphorical and subtly subversive poetry. His work often examined themes of freedom, power, and belonging, drawing attention during Malawi's one-party era.

The Malawi Writers Union of Academic and Non-fiction Authors paid tribute to Mapanje, hailing his significant contributions to scholarship and literature. His acclaimed collections include "Of Chameleons and Gods" and "The Chattering Wagtails of Mikuyu Prison." His memoir, "And Crocodiles Are Hungry at Night," detailed his experiences of imprisonment, exile, and resilience.

Mapanje's legacy will endure through his body of work and his example as a writer who used language for artistic expression and quiet defiance. For many readers, students, and writers, his influence is profound.

mw.headline: Malawi farmers need irrigation equipment
mw.dek: Nsanje District farmers can only cultivate half of their land due to a lack of water pumps.
paragraphs: Farmers in Traditional Authority Malemia, Nsanje District, are appealing for irrigation equipment to increase their crop yields. The scheme's chairperson, Mzinga Mulaphandevu, stated on Tuesday that insufficient materials prevent them from using 30 hectares of land, with only 15 hectares currently cultivated. Farmers expressed a desire for more solar-powered water pumps to support irrigation efforts.

Mulaphandevu highlighted that irrigation offers a reliable harvest compared to unpredictable rainfall. Gloria Genti, a farmer from Chipwembwe Village, reported harvesting 12 to 16 bags of maize, 10 bags of rice, and five bags of beans from her plot. However, Mercy Goliati from Lazao Village noted that the current mobile solar-powered pump system requires significant manual labour.

Collins Walasi, an agriculture development officer for Zunde Extension Planning Area, confirmed that farmers are eager to cultivate the entire scheme but lack the necessary equipment. He mentioned that farmers previously used watering cans before Concern Worldwide recently provided a mobile solar-powered pump system.

ml.headline: Mali military court hears eight cases
ml.dek: Accused include officers and civilians facing charges from desertion to fraud.
paragraphs: The Military Court of Bamako heard eight cases on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, involving military personnel and civilians. The hearings, presided over by magistrate Assama Dolo, addressed charges including fraud, false accusations, and desertion. Some cases involved alleged financial fraud reaching up to six million CFA francs.

Among those accused were Adjudant-Chef Major Oumar Ahmadou MAIGA and Adjudant Moussa DIANE, facing charges such as loss of arms and violation of military orders. Adjudant Yacouba TOGOLA was prosecuted for prisoner escape and related violations, receiving a six-month suspended sentence. Lieutenant-colonel Ogobara GUINDO, deputy prosecutor, stated that these hearings occur twice monthly.

Guindo urged soldiers to maintain discipline and warned against fraudulent recruitment practices where individuals solicit money for integration into the Malian Armed Forces. He stressed that such acts are punishable offenses. The court deferred judgment on some cases while proceeding with others.

ml.headline: Mali hosts FMI delegation to discuss technical aid
ml.dek: The International Monetary Fund's West Africa technical assistance center director met with Mali's finance minister to identify aid needs.
paragraphs: Mali's Minister of Economy and Finance met with a delegation from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on April 11, 2026. The delegation was led by Mr. Christian Ebeke, Director of the IMF's Regional Technical Assistance Center for West Africa (AFRITAC West). The meeting aimed to introduce the new AFRITAC West Director to Malian authorities and discuss Mali's technical assistance requirements.

Discussions focused on identifying the technical assistance needs of key Malian structures. Preparations for the next AFRITAC West Steering Committee meeting, scheduled for Bamako in June 2027, were also discussed. Mali will preside over this upcoming meeting. The meeting reinforced the partnership between Mali and the IMF to improve institutional capacity and public finance management.

The IMF delegation included Mr. Celaine Ngotta Kouame, an economist, and Mr. Moez Ben Hassin, the IMF Resident Representative in Mali. This visit signifies a shared commitment to strengthening Mali's financial governance.

mr.headline: Germany funds 15 million euros for Mauritanian jobs
mr.dek: Nouakchott and Berlin sign financing agreement to support small and medium enterprises.
paragraphs: Mauritania's Minister of Economic Affairs and Development, Mouhamedou Ahmedou Mhaimid, signed a 15 million euro financing agreement in Nouakchott on Tuesday. The deal with Sonja Haus, regional advisor for the German development bank KfW, aims to support employment in Mauritania by financing small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The funds, equivalent to approximately 675 million Mauritanian Ouguiya (MRU), will provide financial resources to foster value creation, growth, and job creation within these businesses.

Minister Mhaimid stated that Mauritania and Germany share a strong partnership across economic and social sectors, highlighting employment as a key area of cooperation. He noted that mobilizing resources remains a challenge for SMEs. The German Ambassador stated the agreement strengthens bilateral relations and reflects a mutual desire for continued partnership based on trust and open dialogue, expressing hope for improved living conditions for young Mauritanians.

The financing agreement is intended to provide SMEs with the financial resources they need. This initiative is expected to contribute to the improvement of living conditions for young Mauritanians. The partnership between Mauritania and Germany is described as solid and fruitful in multiple economic and social areas.

mu.headline: Mauritius ranks second in African governance index
mu.dek: The nation maintains its strong institutional standing but sees a decline in its overall score over a decade.
paragraphs: Mauritius has retained its second-place position in the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance (IIAG), scoring 75.0 out of 100 for the 2016-2025 period. This score places the island nation significantly above the continental average of 50.1 and the Eastern Africa average of 47.5. It ranks just behind Seychelles (78.6) and ahead of Cape Verde (70.3).

Despite its high ranking, the report highlights a net decline of 1.9 points in Mauritius's governance score over the decade, placing its trajectory in the 'Bouncing Back' category. This overall decrease, which saw Seychelles overtake Mauritius for the top spot after an 8.3-point increase, is attributed to erosions in security, rule of law, participation, rights, and inclusion. Areas like media freedom and civil society space have seen their margins shrink.

The IIAG report reveals that 30 African countries improved their governance scores between 2016 and 2025, with the continent's average rising by 0.8 points to 50.1. However, Mauritius is among six top-ranked nations whose 2025 score is lower than their 2016 score. Advances in telecommunications, internet access, and port infrastructure remain key strengths for the island.

The session focused on managing irrigation deficits, controlling pesticide use, and addressing daily operational challenges. Minister Boolell stressed the need for local research and practical solutions, encouraging youth to join the sector.

To support agricultural expansion, 257.9 hectares of land will be allocated to planters under a new roadmap for project distribution. A consultant will also assist pig farmers with operational optimization. Discussions with India are underway to expedite the recruitment of agricultural labor.

mu.headline: Sergeant refuses to attend shooting inquiry reconstitution
mu.dek: Key witnesses recreated the events of October 9 when Elodie Thomas was shot.
paragraphs: An inquiry into a shooting that critically injured Elodie Thomas on October 9 in Camp-Levieux has been complicated by the refusal of Sergeant Gautam Singh Taukoor to participate in a fact reconstitution. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC), led by Satish Faugoo and Hisham Oozeer, organised the event on November 4.

Sergeant Taukoor, the suspect in the shooting, declined to attend the reconstitution. Instead, key witnesses, including Rudy Soobrayen, the van driver, and another employee from the Tribeca Winners supermarket, recreated the events for investigators. Elodie Thomas's colleague also provided details of the incident.
The reconstitution aimed to clarify the sequence of events on the night Thomas was shot. The IPCC is continuing its investigation into the incident.

mu.headline: Mauritius tourism operators train for sustainable practices
mu.dek: The Tourism Authority and OIF are equipping hotels and guesthouses with tools for environmental and economic resilience.
paragraphs: Mauritius's tourism industry is adopting greener practices following a workshop on sustainable initiatives held on November 4 at the Trou aux Biches Beachcomber Golf Resort & Spa. The Tourism Authority, in partnership with the Organisation internationale de la francophonie (OIF), organised the event to guide accommodation providers in integrating environmental, social, and economic sustainability into their daily operations. Participants received practical tools and knowledge to implement more responsible and efficient management models.

Niven Muneesamy, director of the Tourism Authority, highlighted the essential role of guesthouses, tourist residences, and small hotels in diversifying guest experiences and supporting local economies. He stated that sustainable development is an unavoidable issue facing climate change, environmental degradation, and natural resource pressures. Muneesamy also pointed to global geopolitical tensions, such as the Middle East crisis, and rising costs for fuel, electricity, and food as significant financial pressures on tourism businesses.

The workshop aimed to equip operators with concrete knowledge for more effective and responsible management. The initiative supports the island's tourism sector in navigating contemporary challenges, including environmental concerns and economic strains.

mz.headline: Mozambique releases $50 million for fuel imports
mz.dek: Minister Estevão Pale announced measures to ease fuel supply constraints following international market disruptions.
paragraphs: Mozambique's government has made US$50 million available to address ongoing fuel supply constraints, Minister Estevão Pale announced in Parliament. The country faces shortages due to a combination of internal and external factors, including reliance on imports and international market disruptions.

Pale explained that approximately 80% of Mozambique's petroleum products are imported from the Middle East, which experienced escalated conflict and supply chain disruptions in March 2026. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz further increased costs and logistical challenges, while difficulties in securing import financing also impacted distribution companies' capacity.

Cross-border demand also contributes to the shortage, as Mozambique's lower fuel prices encourage smuggling into neighbouring countries. Some fuel unloaded at ports remains under financial retention, with ownership held by suppliers until payments are regularised.

mz.headline: Mozambican engineers to drill Coral North wells
mz.dek: Empresa Nacional de Hidrocarbonetos will gain technical experience through a 10-month campaign to complete six wells.
paragraphs: Mozambican engineers and specialists will participate in drilling and completing six wells for the Coral North gas project over 10 months. Empresa Nacional de Hidrocarbonetos (ENH), through ENH Serviços and its joint venture with Saipem, is moving beyond its traditional role as a statutory shareholder.

ENH has stated ambitions to undertake technical work and compete for contracts, rather than solely holding state interests in petroleum projects. This campaign offers an opportunity to begin demonstrating that shift, providing ENH personnel with practical knowledge beyond reports or training.

The company has spent decades holding state interests in projects operated by international companies. These stakes provide Mozambique with a claim on future profits and a seat in project structures, but have not necessarily built the technical capacity to develop the country’s resources.

na.headline: Dangote launches N$41.6 billion pipeline project in Walvis Bay
na.dek: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote promises cheaper fuel for Namibia with a new N$41.6 billion pipeline project.
paragraphs: Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote launched a N$41.6 billion regional pipeline project near Walvis Bay yesterday. The project by Dangote Industries Limited aims to create a petroleum storage and distribution facility with pipeline infrastructure to improve fuel access across Namibia and landlocked regional countries.

Dangote told Namibians that the project, which includes a 600 million litre storage facility for diesel and petrol, will reduce fuel supply costs. He assured President Netumbo-Nandi Ndaitwah that petroleum prices would become much cheaper. The development also features truck-loading facilities and an approximately 1,700-kilometre regional pipeline network.

The pipeline is planned to extend from Walvis Bay to Otjiwarongo, Rundu, and Francistown, Botswana, serving Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo. President Ndaitwah revealed she personally intervened to prevent bureaucracy from causing Namibia to lose this strategic investment.

na.headline: Namibia launches state-owned air ambulance service
na.dek: The new service aims to reduce travel time for critically ill patients from remote areas to hospitals.
paragraphs: Namibia has launched its first state-owned air ambulance service to transport critically ill and injured patients from remote areas to referral hospitals. Vice president Lucia Witbooi officially launched the service in Windhoek on Wednesday, stating it would address challenges posed by long distances. The service includes a Learjet air ambulance equipped with advanced medical equipment and will collaborate with police and defence forces for helicopter evacuations.

Witbooi said the service would connect patients in remote areas to advanced medical care, reducing gruelling road journeys to minutes or a few hours. Specialised medical personnel will provide critical care during transfers, facilitated by dedicated emergency service centres at referral hospitals. The Government Air Transport Services, along with ministries of works, transport, health, and social services, will provide air emergency units and pilots.

The air ambulance service complements Namibia’s existing ground fleet and strengthens referral pathways between hospitals. Witbooi warned that success depends on sustained funding, aircraft maintenance, training, and safety standards, calling for systems to monitor performance and ensure accountability.

na.headline: Windhoek starts utility disconnections for unpaid bills
na.dek: Human rights lawyer Norman Tjombe questions the legality of cutting off water and electricity to residents and businesses with outstanding municipal accounts.
paragraphs: The City of Windhoek began disconnecting water and electricity services on Thursday for residents and businesses with outstanding municipal bills. The municipality stated that the disconnections, which affect customers across all suburbs, are part of its credit control policy and municipal laws. Customers are urged to settle their accounts or make payment arrangements to avoid losing essential services.

Human rights lawyer Norman Tjombe challenged the legality of the mass disconnections, warning that cutting off water could violate constitutional rights and expose vulnerable populations to health risks like cholera and typhoid. He noted the disconnections are insensitive given the financial pressures from the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, which has impacted rural livelihoods and employment in the meat industry.

The municipality's spokesperson, Lydia Amutenya, stated the disconnections were prompted by continued non-payment and growing debt. Namibia's Water Resources Management Act recognizes equitable access to safe drinking water as a basic human right, while local authorities also have powers to disconnect services for non-payment.
